catalog_quote: All words in Slovene that are not clitics have at least one prominent syllable. Prominence is lexically determined, i.e., it is not predictable, so it is a feature of the word which must be learned along with the segmental sequence and the meaning. Prominence is marked in at least two broadly different ways depending on which dialect area a Slovene speaker comes from. Speakers from Ljubljana, the Upper and Lower Carniolan dialects, or the Carinthian dialect may have a pitch-accent (“tonemic”) system. Speakers from other areas generally have a dynamic stress (“stress”) system. In both the tonemic and stress systems, vestiges of a quantity opposition in stressed syllables may still be realized in many speakers’ systems. sweep_summary: Three title-hits for Slovenian. (1) Greenberg 2003 (STUF) — obtained (KU ScholarWorks copy via the Internet Archive; KU blocks our network) and read: word stress is assigned by a morpheme-level lexical accent algorithm (stress on the first rising-accented morpheme, falling accent shifts right, short final stress retracts), stress is not fixed to any position, and stress placement is the primary word-prosodic contrast in every Slovene system — CONFIRMS the catalog's 'lexical' coding (same author as the deciding Greenberg 2006 grammar; peer-reviewed corroboration, does not supersede the grammar's plainer statement). (2) Šekli 2010 (SSJLK 46, open PDF from centerslo.si; Šekli sole author, Smole is the compilers) — read: Standard Slovene verb stress is organized into lexical accent paradigms with root vs. infinitive/present-suffix stress and infinitive/present alternations (mériti mérim, nosíti nósim, moríti morím); REFINES the catalog's classification with the morphological structure of verb stress. (3) Vermeer 1986 (De Gruyter sandhi volume) — paywalled (30 EUR, no repository copy, no abstract); comparative prosodic-sandhi accentology, unlikely to be the best stress statement; priority low. discovery used Unpaywall/OpenAlex/OpenAIRE/Semantic Scholar APIs and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: In the illustrative wordlists and the transcribed passage below certain syllables have been marked as stressed. These stressed syllables are characterized by greater duration as well as by amplitude and pitch prominence. Non-compound words have no more than one stressed syllable. Stress placement is not predictable but is also rarely distinctive in Slovene, although in a few instances different forms of the same noun or verb differ only in stress placement, e.g.: ['stua:ri], [stua'ri:], stvari ('things', dual vs plural), ['no:simo], [no'si:mo], nosimo ('carry' 1st p. pl. indicative and imperative). [p. 88] Standard Slovene distinguishes two pitch accents, traditionally referred to as the 'acute' and the 'circumflex' accents, and these accents are tied to the location of stress. [p. 89]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Standard Slovene (Ljubljana speakers) has one stressed syllable per non-compound word; its position is not predictable from phonological form (so it must be learned lexically) and is only rarely contrastive, though minimal pairs exist (stvari dual vs plural, nosimo indicative vs imperative). Stressed vowels are long, unstressed short (length no longer distinctive for most speakers). On the stressed syllable two pitch accents (acute = rising/low, circumflex = falling/high) are distinguished, tied to the stress location, seldom lexically distinctive, and some standard speakers lack the distinction.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the authors state only that non-compound words have no more than one stressed syllable (compounds implicitly may have more).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-only minimal pairs: stvari ['stua:ri] dual vs [stua'ri:] plural; nosimo ['no:simo] indicative vs [no'si:mo] imperative. pitch accent minimal pair kila 'hernia' (acute) vs kila 'kilo' (circumflex); many words vary in accent and some speakers make no accent distinction.

new_statements.quote: Stress may either occur on the root syllable or on the theme-vowel: however, the phonological properties of the formed word have no clear correlation with stress assignment, which implies that these different positions of stress assignment do not seem to be triggered by any phonological factor. Rather, different stress patterns correlate either with specific roots, or with specific morphosyntactic constructions. This situates the regulation of stress assignment in NM Slovenian in the domain of morphosyntactic (i.e. lexical) specification. [pp. 49-50] [...] Similar to Standard Slovenian, NM Slovenian seems to place a tone on the stressed syllable of the word, but the final post-stressed syllable in the word bears a 'boundary tone', viz. it receives the opposite tone value of the one realized on the stressed syllable [p. 20]

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (lexical, morphologically governed stress with pitch accent), stated for the Novo mesto dialect rather than the standard; adds the root-vs-theme stress classes, variable stress, the m.sg root-stress rule and the tone/boundary-tone description, and corroborates Greenberg 2003 and Šekli 2010 on morphological stress alternations in verbs.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Novo mesto (Dolenjska) Slovenian the position of stress is not set by any phonological factor: it is specified lexically by root and by morphological class/construction (root stress vs. theme-vowel stress in participles, with some roots variable between the two, e.g. ['jòkalá] ~ [jo'kàlá]); the masculine singular participle takes root stress by a morphological rule. A high or low tone is lexically specified on the stressed syllable and the word-final syllable carries the opposite, predictable boundary tone. Length is at best marginal and confined to stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (only boundary tone on the word-final post-stressed syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Variable stress for some roots (jòk- 'cry' root or theme stress); m.sg participles take root stress even in theme-stressed paradigms except with some roots (kàd- 'smoke' allows theme stress in m.sg, dùb- 'get' does not).

tone_statements.quote: Standard Slovene distinguishes rising and falling tone in long syllables. Quantity outside of the stressed syllable has been lost, and all non-final stressed syllables have been lengthened. This means that short stress is only found on the final syllable of a word. In final position the original acute and the neo-acute on etymologically short vowels are short falling. ... The original circumflex in Slovene is realized as long and falling ... The northeastern Slovene dialects discussed here do not have distinctive pitch oppositions.
tone_statements.locator: p. 64, opening paragraph; last sentence from p. 69 footnote 2
tone_statements.summary: Historical accentology: Standard Slovene has rising vs falling tone on long (stressed) syllables; the Haloze/NE Slovene dialects documented have lost pitch (marks = length).

tone_statements.quote: This study was performed as a means of confirming or refuting Zorko’s claims about an unusually archaic prosodic system in Haloze. On the other hand, although the situation is not completely as one might expect for a Styrian dialect, there is no distinctive tone in Haloze. tone_statements.quote: Dobro znano je, da ima slovenski jezik (njega del seveda) tonemsko nasprotje, npr. lipo (Asg) — lîpo (Isg) besede lipa (Nsg). Čeprav sta ta dva naglasna načina — prvega bomo imenovali akutiranega, drugega cirkumflektiranega — bila ugotovljena že pred več kot 150 leti ... je treba vendarle reči, da v svojem jedru vse do danes fonetično nista zadovoljivo pojasnjena. ... Desto wichtiger ist Mitja Sovre's Feststellung, dass der Gegensatz zwischen dem Akut und dem Zirkumflex als Tonhöhenunterschied aufzufassen ist.
tone_statements.translation: It is well known that Slovene (part of it, of course) has a tonemic opposition, e.g. lipo (Asg) — lîpo (Isg) of the word lipa (Nsg). Although these two accent types — we shall call the first acute, the second circumflex — were established more than 150 years ago ... it must be said that at their core they have to this day not been satisfactorily explained phonetically. ... All the more important is Sovre's finding that the opposition between acute and circumflex is to be understood as a pitch-height difference.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemic accents (acute, circumflex) on long stressed syllables; author: contrast is pitch height (acute low, basic shape concave; circumflex high, convex), shapes vary with sentence intonation; short stress only delimitative.

tone_statements.quote: V slovenskem knjižnem jeziku se dopuščata dva tipa naglasa: dinamični in tonemski. Pri tonemskem naglaševanju ločimo na naglašenih vokalih dve intonaciji, ki ju tradicionalno imenujemo rastoča in padajoča. ... ju je bolje imenovati kar po znakih, s katerima ju označujemo: akutirana namesto rastoča in cirkumflektirana namesto padajoča. Cirkumflektirana intonacija je fonološko neoznačen tonem, akutirana pa označen (markiran) ... Ker je tonemsko naglaševanje v slovenskem knjižnem jeziku samo fakultativno, se mu navadno ne posveča dosti pozornosti.
tone_statements.translation: In the Slovene standard language two types of accent are admitted: dynamic and tonemic. In tonemic accentuation we distinguish on the stressed vowels two intonations, traditionally called rising and falling. ... it is better to name them simply after the signs with which we mark them: acute instead of rising and circumflex instead of falling. The circumflex intonation is the phonologically unmarked toneme, the acute the marked one ... Since tonemic accentuation is only optional in the Slovene standard language, it is usually not given much attention.
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemes (acute, circumflex) on the stressed vowel; tonemic accent optional beside dynamic; final/only short syllables circumflex only; at least ~600 tone-marked forms in the paradigms.

tone_statements.quote: There are two prosodically distinct dialect types, the tonal or pitch-accent Slovene and the non-tonal or stress-accent Slovene (Toporišič, 2004 [1976]; Šuštaršič & Tivadar, 2001). sources.quote: Standard Slovene distinguishes rising and falling tone in long syllables. Quantity outside of the stressed syllable has been lost, and all non-final stressed syllables have been lengthened. This means that short stress is only found on the final syllable of a word. In final position the original acute and the neo-acute on etymologically short vowels are short falling. ... The original circumflex in Slovene is realized as long and falling ... The northeastern Slovene dialects discussed here do not have distinctive pitch oppositions.

sources.note: Historical accentology: Standard Slovene has rising vs falling tone on long (stressed) syllables; the Haloze/NE Slovene dialects documented have lost pitch (marks = length).

sources.quote: This study was performed as a means of confirming or refuting Zorko’s claims about an unusually archaic prosodic system in Haloze. On the one hand, the phonetic analysis did show that quantity is distinctive in eastern Haloze. ... On the other hand, although the situation is not completely as one might expect for a Styrian dialect, there is no distinctive tone in Haloze. There is only one pattern of pitch contour on short syllables. It is rising. ... I discovered that the exact same pattern of pitch contour occurred on long as the one found on short.

tone.translation: It is well known that Slovene (part of it, of course) has a tonemic opposition, e.g. lipo (Asg) — lîpo (Isg) of the word lipa (Nsg). tone.translation: In the Slovene standard language two types of accent are admitted: dynamic and tonemic. In tonemic accentuation we distinguish on the stressed vowels two intonations, traditionally called rising and falling. ... it is better to name them simply after the signs with which we mark them: acute instead of rising and circumflex instead of falling. The circumflex intonation is the phonologically unmarked toneme, the acute the marked one ... Since tonemic accentuation is only optional in the Slovene standard language, it is usually not given much attention.
